core: The historical origin of the concept: Goethe's Weltliteratur ('world literature')
World literature as literature in translation and circulation beyond its place of origin (Damrosch's 'mode of circulation and of reading' framing)
Why translation is central: reading in translation is the norm; translators make interpretive choices that shape the work

Anchor texts and traditions: Epic of Gilgamesh, Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, Mahabharata and Ramayana, Tale of Genji, One Thousand and One Nights, Don Quixote, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Achebe, Marquez, Murakami (named briefly)
The risks of a survey: canon formation, western-centrism, treating cultures as homogeneous (presented as attributed scholarly debates)
The value of comparative reading (value and habit, not the comparison method)
supporting: Goethe's biography and the status of Faust as 'sometimes considered Germany's greatest contribution to world literature' (Britannica)
Damrosch's critique of the older European-centered canon of world literature in North America
Regional and chronological breadth of open anthologies (NOVA; LibreTexts Compact Anthology)
outOfScope: American literature survey (sibling topic american-literature-overview; this lesson stays non-U.S.-focused)
Fiction, poetry, and drama as forms (sibling form topics)

claims.claim: The name and the concept of Weltliteratur (world literature) come from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe; the NOVA open textbook World Literature states that 'both the name and the concept of Weltliteratur (world literature) come from him.'

Goethe (1749-1832) was a German poet, playwright, and novelist; his Faust, a play about a man who sells his soul to the Devil, is 'sometimes considered Germany's greatest contribution to world literature' (Britannica).

David Damrosch (What Is World Literature?, 2003) defines world literature as 'not a canon of texts but a mode of circulation and of reading,' arguing that 'world literature is work that gains in translation'; a work becomes world literature by circulating across languages and readerships rather than by membership in a fixed list.

World literature 'was long defined in North America as an established canon of European masterpieces,' and an emerging global perspective has challenged both that European focus and the very category of 'the masterpiece' (Damrosch).

World literature surveys conventionally include anchor texts from many regions and eras: the Epic of Gilgamesh (Mesopotamia), Homer's Iliad and Odyssey (Greece), the Mahabharata and the Ramayana (South Asia), the Tale of Genji (Japan), One Thousand and One Nights (Arabic tradition), Don Quixote (Spain), and modern authors including Tolstoy, Achebe, Marquez, and Murakami — all present in the NOVA open anthology's table of contents; the LibreTexts Compact Anthology similarly spans the Middle East and Near East, Greece, China, India, Rome, and later centuries.

Fyodor Dostoevsky and Leo Tolstoy are standard presences in reference surveys of world literature: Britannica's Russian literature article gives each its own 19th-century section, and the NOVA anthology includes a Tolstoy chapter.

Translation is central to world literature: most readers meet foreign works in translation, and translation involves interpretive choices — Damrosch observes that foreign works 'have often been distorted by the immediate needs of their own editors and translators.'

Survey anthologies present their selections as representative of many cultures whose works examine themes that cross cultural boundaries, while each selection also 'illuminates its particular cultural, historical, and social context' (LibreTexts Compact Anthology introduction).

Comparative reading across traditions is valuable because works change as they move between cultures: Damrosch describes world literature as an 'elliptical space created between the source and receiving cultures,' where works mean one thing at home and something related but different abroad.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What 'world literature' is: a canon of masterpieces vs. a mode of circulation.
positions: Older usage (as Damrosch describes it): world literature 'was long defined in North America as an established canon of European masterpieces.'
Damrosch (2003): world literature is 'not a canon of texts but a mode of circulation and of reading.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses Damrosch's circulation-and-reading definition as its analytical frame and presents the European-canon view as the historical position his work critiques, so students see the definition as a scholarly argument rather than a settled fact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does translation help or harm works of world literature?
positions: Damrosch: 'world literature is work that gains in translation' — translation is what allows circulation and new life.
Damrosch: foreign works 'can be seriously mishandled' and 'have often been distorted by the immediate needs of their own editors and translators.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a contradiction: circulation in translation enables access while altering the work. The lesson teaches both halves — translation is the norm and a gain, and it always involves interpretive choices with real consequences.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How representative is a survey's list of texts?
positions: Anthology editors (NOVA; LibreTexts) present selections as representative of many cultures and of themes that cross cultural boundaries.
Scholarly critique (Damrosch): single works can be distorted in circulation and the old lists were European-centered, so one or two texts cannot stand in for a whole culture.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps both: surveys sample and organize, and readers should treat that compression as a limitation — a tool for orientation, not a portrait of a culture.

sourceRecords.title: What Is World Literature? (David Damrosch, Princeton University Press, 2003)
sourceRecords.notes: Author abstract read via the OpenAlex API record (api.openalex.org/works/https://doi.org/10.2307/40157771) on 2026-08-21. Confirms: world literature is 'not a canon of texts but a mode of circulation and of reading'; 'world literature is work that gains in translation'; it 'was long defined in North America as an established canon of European masterpieces'; works move into 'an elliptical space created between the source and receiving cultures'; foreign works 'have often been distorted by the immediate needs of their own editors and translators' and 'can be seriously mishandled in the process.' Only abstract-level claims were used; the book itself was not read in full.
